headline: Preserve conceptual positions while normalizing each level
statement: Return the maximum width of a binary tree. Width counts positions between the leftmost and rightmost non-null nodes at a depth, including gaps where nodes would occur in a complete binary tree.
intuition: Width includes empty positions between real nodes. Give nodes the positions they would have in a complete binary tree, then measure the distance from the first to last position at each level. Subtract the level's starting position to keep the numbers small without changing the gaps.
approach: Queue pairs of node and conceptual position.
For each level, remember its first position and process the original queue length.
Normalize positions relative to that first value and enqueue children at 2i and 2i+1.
The final normalized position plus one is this level’s width.
correctness: Complete-tree indices preserve every horizontal gap. BFS orders a level left to right, so its first and final positions bound exactly the required width. Subtracting a common offset preserves differences; generating children after normalization shifts every next-level index by the same amount, again preserving differences. The maximum computed width is therefore correct.
bruteForce: Build the complete-tree slots explicitly, including every null position. Sparse trees can require exponentially many empty slots.

complexity.explanation: w_real is the maximum number of present nodes at any depth, not the conceptual width including gaps. Only real nodes are enqueued; during a level transition the queue holds parts of two adjacent levels, still O(w_real). Normalization avoids coordinate growth caused solely by a deep one-sided path.

pitfalls: Width includes missing positions between real nodes.
Queue length is not the width.
Normalize every level before calculating child indices.
